cells.tense: You are standing where something you pictured is coming in.
cells.act: find the rhythm and stay in it
cells.ask: Answer what is already yours the same way each day this week — no burst on strong days, no stalling on flat ones.
cells.core:
Something you pictured has been arriving. It comes in at a pace you can hold — you are not dragging it forward or holding it back. Wanting and doing point the same direction, and that steadiness is yours, not a mood passing through. The thing keeps moving even when you say nothing about it.

This week, hold the pace rather than improve it. Answer what is already yours the same way each day — no surge of effort, no day off, no announcement. What you get at the end is not a larger version of it; it is finding out that steady was what it wanted. You are the one who kept the rhythm.
cells.sheetLine: What you pictured is arriving, and you meet it steadily.
cells.verb: meeting what has been fully imagined and felt as it arrives
cells.place: the threshold where what was outside is entering now

cells.tense: You will be reaching for the next arrival before this one has landed.
cells.ask: Give the good that has come in a fixed moment of tending this week, then keep your hands off, letting it be exactly what it is.
cells.core:
Something you imagined is coming in, and a hand is already on the next thing. The good one behind you has not had a day free of adjusting. Holding it open keeps it from being what it is, because the moment you stop shaping it, it is real and you are no longer needed at the door. Tightness reads as care from the inside. From the outside, it looks like nothing is permitted to arrive.

Try this week giving the good that has come in a fixed moment of tending, then keeping your hands off for the rest. Let it be exactly what it is right now. If it does not need something, do not hand it something to need. What you practice is holding what is yours without your whole weight on it.
cells.sheetLine: You're gripping it before it has landed.

cells.tense: You were at the door when it opened, and you are still describing the room.
cells.act: write both sides of it on one page and close the page
cells.ask: Put what seems settled and what does not on a single page, then close it, and open it again only the next morning.
cells.core:
Something has waited at your door long enough that you have started waiting with it. You know there is something out there. Letting it in means it is here and settled, and staying in the not-yet has been easier than arriving. The hotter and colder you run about it, the less you say. The feeling has not left. The move toward meeting what is coming has gone quiet.

This week, take something you keep turning over and put both sides on a single page — what seems settled, what does not — then close it and open it again only the next morning. You are not deciding. You are letting what you carry stand still long enough to look at. When you open it, one side may have less to say.

cells.tense: You are meeting what arrives without knowing you are the one meeting it.
cells.act: refine one distinction by close attention
cells.ask: Study a small detail of what has arrived, closely, with nothing to decide or fix, and see what you can now tell apart.
cells.core:
This is already happening. Something is being met at your door and you are answering it, but the answering gets filed under circumstance. The timing happened to work, the day happened to be kind, someone happened to call. What does not get counted is the part where you saw it coming and made room. The meeting is real, and the name on it is missing.

Small and specific. Study a small detail of what has arrived, closely, with nothing to decide afterward. The aim is not to solve it — it is to catch yourself noticing what you can already tell apart. Once you catch that, the timing starts looking like yours again.
